tier_reason: Comparison.jpg is a bar chart (y-axis scale, no value labels) of OpenCV GaussianBlur vs three tutorial stages, produced by the public harness parallel_processing/main.cpp with flags in parallel_processing/CMakeLists.txt, GCC 6.3 and a Raspberry Pi 3B+; it falls short of A because the OpenCV version, build options and thread count are not stated and the numbers exist only as chart bars read by eye.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Numbers exist only as bars in Comparison.jpg (y-axis scale in ms, no value labels), so values are read off the chart and approximate. Final stage (memory management + SIMD + OpenMP) about 3.4 ms vs OpenCV about 8.9 ms at 720x720, about 7.9 vs 19.8 ms at 1080x1080, about 13.7 vs 35 ms at 1440x1440, roughly 2.5x (derived from page data). The single-thread stages are slower than OpenCV at every size: memory management about 11.6 / 26.9 / 48.4 ms and memory management + SIMD about 10.0 / 23.3 / 41.5 ms vs OpenCV 8.9 / 19.8 / 35 ms.
corrections.workload: 5x5 Gaussian blur (sigma 1.0, BORDER_REPLICATE) of a single-channel CV_32F image: the repo's 720x720 image.jpg, with 1080x1080 and 1440x1440 obtained by enabling the commented-out resize line in main.cpp; mean of 100 back-to-back iterations per variant timed with std::chrono, no warm-up, on a Raspberry Pi 3B+.
corrections.caveats: Tutorial rather than a library (About: 'Step-by-step tutorial for optimizing a Gaussian image smoothing function'). The win comes only from the OpenMP stage spreading middle rows across the Pi's cores; the project's own single-thread SIMD stage is slower than OpenCV at all three sizes, and the OpenCV version, build options and thread count are not stated. The harness never checks the output against OpenCV's (it only shows the result with imshow). CMakeLists sets -O3 -Ofast -funroll-loops (-fopenmp for the parallel stage) but no -mfpu=neon on a 32-bit OS, so whether the cv::v_float32x4 code, and the OpenCV baseline, actually ran NEON is not stated. Minor code issues: the top-row 'leftovers' loop redeclares j and recomputes the whole row in scalar, and the vector loops assume a width divisible by 4. Kernel weights are hard-coded for sigma 1.0 and a 5x5 kernel only. No license file (raw LICENSE and LICENSE.md are 404), so reference only. Last commit 2021-03-25. Gaussian blur is an image filter, only loosely in color-and-resampling.

notes: Chart values match the record; harness and flags read in parallel_processing/main.cpp, Gaussian_refinement5.hpp and the three CMakeLists. imrid.net blog posts not opened (blogs blocked). Metadata confirmed: 25 stars, 6 forks, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2021-03-25, no license.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine tables in readme.md with the CPU model (i7-4700HQ) but no benchmark script in the repo (scripts/ holds only build.sh), no Go toolchain version or flags and no odiff version, so C.

corrections.hardware: Linux, Intel Core i7-4700HQ @ 2.40GHz (README says '8 cores'; the i7-4700HQ has 4 cores and 8 hardware threads, and imgdiff starts runtime.NumCPU() goroutines)
corrections.caveats: Multi-core vs single-thread: pkg/imgdiff/imgdiff.go splits rows over runtime.NumCPU() goroutines and cmd/main.go decodes both PNGs concurrently, while odiff bills itself as the fastest one-thread tool. The two tools also did different output work. imgdiff's default output is a transparent mask with red pixels written with png.BestSpeed, while odiff's default writes the base image with the diff overlaid. In the benchmark-era build (commit 1be7ce7, 2020-12-14), main.go deferred writer.Flush() and f.Close() and then left through os.Exit(1), which skips deferred calls, so the last buffered bytes of every diff PNG were never written. The output was truncated until the 'fix writing output' commit on 2021-03-25. imgdiff has no anti-aliasing detection, reads pixels through the generic image.At interface, and its loops run one row and column past the bounds (harmless). The odiff build is unversioned: imgdiff measured odiff at 6.475 s on the cypress pair, while odiff's own README reports 1.168 s for the same pair on a different machine, so imgdiff probably tested an older odiff. odiff has since been rewritten in Zig with SIMD, so the gap is probably gone. The author writes that imgdiff 'isn't as fast as a tool like this should be'. Benchmark code is not in the repo (only the tables), and the toolchain and flags are not stated. Last commit 2021-03-25. Image comparison is only loosely in color-and-resampling; consider the image category.

notes: README numbers match the record, and its relative column matches its own means (6.475/1.442 = 4.49, 6.016/1.908 = 3.15, derived from page data); the mismatching relative column belongs to odiff, not imgdiff. The output-truncation bug is confirmed by comparing raw cmd/main.go at 1be7ce7 with HEAD. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 1.7k stars, 69 forks, 7 commits, release v1.0.0, last commit 2021-03-25.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine tables in README.md, with the exact commands in images/README.md and the test images in images/. The machine is named only as a 'MacBook Pro 16' with no CPU model, and the odiff, ImageMagick and pixelmatch versions, compiler and flags are not stated, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: cypress.io screenshots: odiff 1.168 s +/- 0.008 vs ImageMagick compare 8.881 s (README relative 7.65) vs pixelmatch 7.712 s (README relative 6.67). Water image pair: odiff 1.951 s +/- 0.014 vs ImageMagick compare 9.326 s (README relative 5.24) vs pixelmatch 10.614 s (README relative 5.50). The means give 7.60x, 6.60x, 4.78x and 5.44x (derived from page data). README text: 'Odiff is 6 times faster than imagemagick and pixelmatch'.
corrections.workload: Pixel-by-pixel visual diff of two full-page cypress.io screenshots and of the water-4k.png / water-4k-2.png pair (README calls it 8k; 8400 x 4725 per imgdiff's README), writing a diff PNG, timed end to end as separate processes with hyperfine -i (commands in images/README.md).
corrections.caveats: The README tables were last changed on 2021-01-27 (GitHub blame) and were run on macOS 11 Big Sur beta. They therefore measure the OCaml-era odiff, not the current Zig/SIMD code. bench.sh only compares odiff commits with each other and does not rerun ImageMagick or pixelmatch. The README relative column does not match its own means. For the water pair, 9.326/1.951 = 4.78 and 10.614/1.951 = 5.44 against the stated 5.24 and 5.50. For cypress, 8.881/1.168 = 7.60 and 7.712/1.168 = 6.60 against 7.65 and 6.67 (derived from page data). This suggests the rows come from different runs. The README says 'the produced difference will be the same for all 3 commands', but the tools do different work. ImageMagick compare -compose src flags every differing pixel with no YIQ threshold. pixelmatch is a Node.js CLI that runs anti-aliasing detection by default, while odiff leaves it off by default. Discussion #82 (2023) reports 1.07% different pixels from odiff vs 0.75% from pixelmatch and jimp at threshold 0.1. A 2026-08-24 commit (#185) fixes YIQ coefficient rounding that caused systematic under-counting in the current code. The ImageMagick thread count and the CPU model are not stated. Hyperfine wall time includes process start-up, PNG decode and encode. Image comparison is only loosely in color-and-resampling (a color-distance task); consider the image category.

notes: Numbers and the benchmarks.png chart (1.168 s vs 8.881 s) match the record. The record's language is Zig (current code), but the benchmarked build was OCaml. imgdiff (same batch) measured odiff independently at 6.475 s on the cypress pair, but only against imgdiff and on different hardware, so it does not lift odiff to B against ImageMagick. Metadata confirmed: MIT (LICENSE.txt), 3.2k stars, 115 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-24, active.
